problems.title: elite-v2 native-eval (operator selection) ran on train seeds already used for plan search/validation, not on held-out seeds
problems.evidence: The 9 elite-v2 native-eval runs (3,560 episodes) used seeds 1111-1120 (6 runs) and 1121-1127 (3 runs). Every one of those seeds was also a search or validate seed in elite-v2 native-search runs. 1111-1120 were validate seeds in cd2134b9, with 1111-1114 also in 7a005bcc and 3b698f58, and 1115-1120 in fb8a1aac. 1121-1124 were search seeds and 1125-1127 validate seeds in e7bfb9f9, and 1125-1127 were also validate seeds in 3b698f58. This is allowed by the pool rules: all are train seeds and the eval pool 7101-7120 was untouched. But the operator and plan selection evals were not on held-out seeds, so the only held-out measurements before the final are the two rehearsals on 7101-7105. Not a seed-hygiene violation for the final result.

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute the auditor's facts. I re-derived them read-only from the run files.

1. **Eval runs.** There are 9 native-eval runs in runtime/rl/elite-v2/runs, with 3,560 eval_episode rows in total (360+180+160+640+500+250+490+490+490).
   - Six runs (3d26291d, 57681a80, 3579bdc1, 22f5d255, 16458ec5, 5733883c) used seeds 1111-1120 on levels 1-12.
   - Three runs (ba4bfda4, da15d5a7, 237d1813) used seeds 1121-1127 on levels 1-26, except levels 3 and 12.

2. **Search specs.** The search_start specs in native-search events.jsonl match the auditor exactly:
   - cd2134b9 (level 11) validated on 1107-1120.
   - 7a005bcc validated on 1105-1114.
   - 3b698f58 validated on 1109-1114 and 1125-1128.
   - fb8a1aac validated on 1115-1120.
   - e7bfb9f9 searched on 1121-1124 and validated on 1125-1134.
   - The actual search_eval and search_validate episode seeds match these specs. So every eval seed 1111-1127 was a search or validate seed of some elite-v2 native-search run.

3. **Purpose of the evals.** The phase config's native-eval purpose calls 1121-1127 "held-out train seeds … used to choose between operator networks". The episodes confirm that operator choice was made on these runs:
   - Main operators 87a774c6682d, d86c06c72ae1, 92aae749d574 and a4e176d87062 (the one used in the final) were compared on 1111-1120.
   - Elite operators 252d6f389d12 (used in the final) and aadc412442ff were compared on 1121-1127.
   - Plan comparisons (player "plan") were also run on these seeds.

**Where the claim needs refining.** A seed only identifies a game together with its level. Checked at the (seed, level) level, the overlap is smaller than the seed-level wording suggests:
- Only 889 of the 3,560 episodes (about 25%) are on (seed, level) pairs that an earlier elite-v2 search had already played.
  - 700 are level 11 on seeds 1111-1120, validated in cd2134b9 (2026-10-10 20:51, before all those evals).
  - 189 are levels 20, 21 and 22 on seeds 1121-1127, from e7bfb9f9 and 3b698f58, both before the evals.
- The other 2,671 episodes are on pairs never used for search or collection in any phase:
  - campaign-v1 and elite-v1 searches and pools used only 1001-1010.
  - The elite-v2 collect runs used 1001-1010, 1101-1110 and 1131-1135.
- The evals were held out from operator training data. The operator receipts list training runs on seeds 1001-1010, 1101-1110 and 1131-1135 only.

problems.title: Per-decision provenance is stripped from the journal, so 'no plan-executor fallback' rests on the per-game policy name plus the code path
problems.evidence: campaign_run.py lines 287, 354 and 412 journal the result with the 'decisions' key removed: {k: v for k, v in result.items() if k != 'decisions'}. The per-decision 'provenance': 'model:operator:...' field (operator_net.py line 427) therefore never reaches episodes.jsonl. The journal only records the game-level policy name. Two things in the code make a silent fallback implausible. OperatorPolicy.choose always takes the argmax of the network scores, and PlanTracker only supplies an instruction feature. A policy exception voids the episode instead of falling back (episode.py lines 233-237), and no game was voided. Still, this cannot be proven decision by decision from the journal. The summary also records engine_replay_verified=false.

verdict.reasoning:
I re-checked every part of the claim against the files, read-only, and could not refute it.

1) Code. campaign_run.py lines 287, 354 and 412 each journal `{k: v for k, v in result.items() if k != "decisions"}`. These are the star_replay, challenge_attempt and campaign_attempt rows. episode.py line 249 is the only place per-decision provenance is stored, and it goes into the dropped `decisions` list. operator_net.py line 427 sets provenance to `model:{self.name}`.

2) Journal. I streamed the final run's episodes.jsonl (runtime/rl/elite-v2/runs/native-final-af081b54e5f54478aa76b24bc02bdbf5).
- It has 1,144 rows: 267 campaign_attempt, 102 challenge_attempt, 30 star_replay and 745 strategy_decision.
- None of the 399 game results has a `decisions` key. No line in the file contains "provenance".
- events.jsonl holds only game_claimed, upgrades_bought, campaign_start/end, level_blocked, host_features, engine_identity and strategy_brain. None of its lines contains "provenance" or "fallback".
- The only per-decision trace left is result.plan, the executed native actions, plus n_decisions (116,449 in total). Neither records who chose an action.

3) Policy name. Each game records only `policy`:
- main levels 1-12 (65 campaign attempts and 30 star replays) used `operator:a4e176d87062`;
- elite levels 13-26 (202 attempts) and all 102 challenges used `operator:252d6f389d12`.

4) Code path, which supports "no fallback".
- tools/campaign-survey.py lines 1249-1257 build plain `OperatorPolicy(net, genome, name=...)` for both operators, with no wrapper.
- OperatorPolicy.choose (operator_net.py lines 419-429) always returns the argmax of the network scores. operator_net.py contains no try/except.
- PlanTracker.instruction only builds the instruction feature through BuildOrderPolicy._step_option and never returns a choice.
- episode.py lines 233-237 void the episode if the policy raises. All 399 games have status "terminal" with void_reason null, so none was voided.

5) Verification. survey-summary.json and supervisor-receipt.json both show episodes_journal.engine_replay_verified = false (integrity_verified = true). receipt.json shows verified = false. So no cold replay that re-scores the network at each decision was ever run either.

6) The claimed counts match the journal: seed 8101 won 26 distinct levels, and the per-seed totals are 26/25/22/25/22 = 120.

The problem is therefore real and minor. It is a gap in the evidence, not a sign that anything went wrong. The code makes a silent fallback very unlikely, and the counts are right, but the journal cannot show decision by decision that the network made every choice.
verdict.corrected_statement:
Confirmed, minor (an evidence gap, not an error in the result). In the final run native-final-af081b54e5f54478aa76b24bc02bdbf5, all three journal writes in campaign_run.py (lines 287, 354, 412) drop the per-episode "decisions" list. So none of the 116,449 per-decision records reach episodes.jsonl, including their provenance field ("model:operator:<sha12>", operator_net.py line 427 via episode.py line 249). Neither episodes.jsonl nor events.jsonl contains the string "provenance" anywhere.

The claim that every move was made by the network rests on two things only:
- (a) each game's policy name: operator:a4e176d87062 for main levels 1-12 and their star replays (95 games), and operator:252d6f389d12 for elite levels 13-26 and all challenges (304 games);
- (b) the code: tools/campaign-survey.py lines 1249-1257 build plain OperatorPolicy objects; OperatorPolicy.choose always takes the network's argmax; PlanTracker only supplies the instruction feature; operator_net.py has no exception handling; and a policy exception voids the episode (episode.py lines 233-237). All 399 games ended "terminal" with no void_reason.

No per-decision cold replay or re-scoring was run (engine_replay_verified = false; receipt verified = false). Impact on the result: the counts are correct as journaled. Seed 8101 won 26/26, and the per-seed totals 26/25/22/25/22 make 120/130. But "operator network only, no plan-executor fallback" is backed by the code path and per-game policy names, not by journaled per-decision evidence. problems.title: Summary total_stars includes challenge stars; 'failed_level' means the first failed level only

I re-checked the final run's survey-summary.json and streamed episodes.jsonl, all read-only. Every factual claim in the audit holds.

(1) total_stars per seed is 72/73/60/69/62. That equals sum(won.values()) of 61/62/50/58/52 plus challenge_stars of 11/11/10/11/10. In alpharush_rl/campaign_run.py, total_stars() is defined as sum(won.values()) + challenge_stars(won_challenges). When challenges are enabled it overwrites the plain campaign sum (summary["total_stars"] = total_stars()). In alpharush_rl/campaign.py, challenge_stars counts one star per won (level, mode) pair. The challenge_attempt payloads have stars=None.

One nuance: the 'campaign best stars' 61/62/50/58/52 include star_replay improvements. Using campaign_attempt rows alone, the best-star sums are only 58/59/47/52/52. Adding the won star_replay rows reproduces 61/62/50/58/52 exactly.

(2) failed_level is set only once, on the first unwon level (`if failed_level is None: failed_level = level`). For 8105 it is 17, while failed_levels = [17, 19, 22, 26] because a lost elite stage does not end the campaign.

(3) For 8103, attempts has 60 rows. Two of them are non-game blocked rows, {'level':25,'blocked_by':24} and {'level':26,'blocked_by':25}, appended by the prerequisite check. That leaves 58 games, which matches the 58 campaign_attempt rows for 8103 in episodes.jsonl. The other seeds have no extra rows: 37/45/46/81 rows match 37/45/46/81 campaign_attempt rows.

None of this affects the headline result. levels_won counts are 26/25/22/25/22 = 120 of 130. They are independently confirmed from won campaign_attempt rows in episodes.jsonl: 26/25/22/25/22 distinct levels won. Seed 8101 won all of levels 1-26, with failed_levels=[], blocked_levels=[] and completed=True. The issue is real only as a labelling/definition caveat for anyone reading total_stars, failed_level or len(attempts). It is not an error in the claimed result.
verdict.corrected_statement:
The audit's observations are correct, but they are only labelling caveats and do not change the claimed result. In runtime/rl/elite-v2/runs/native-final-af081b54e5f54478aa76b24bc02bdbf5/survey-summary.json, total_stars (72/73/60/69/62) counts the in-game star currency on purpose: total_stars() in alpharush_rl/campaign_run.py adds best campaign stars (61/62/50/58/52) to challenge stars, which are one per won Heroic/Iron mode (11/11/10/11/10). The best campaign stars already include star_replay improvements; from first-clear attempts alone they would be 58/59/47/52/52. So total_stars is not a pure campaign-star score.

failed_level is only the first unwon level. Elite losses do not end a campaign, so failed_levels is the complete list. For example, seed 8105 has failed_level=17 and failed_levels=[17,19,22,26]; seed 8103 has [22,24] plus blocked levels [25,26].

The attempts list for 8103 has 60 rows, but 2 are blocked markers (levels 25 and 26), so there were 58 games. That matches its 58 campaign_attempt rows in episodes.jsonl. The other seeds' attempts lists contain only games.

The headline result is unaffected. Levels won per seed are 26/25/22/25/22 = 120 of 130, and episodes.jsonl confirms this independently. Seed 8101 won all 26 levels, with no failed or blocked levels and completed=True. Any report that quotes stars or attempt counts should say that total_stars includes challenge stars and that attempts include blocked rows.

problems.title: worker-stdout.json differs byte-wise from survey-summary.json though the JSON content is identical
problems.evidence: Both files are 69455 bytes but have different sha256: survey-summary 019af29f... and worker-stdout 511d96fd.... After json.loads the two are equal, so the difference is formatting or key order. The supervisor receipt's summary_sha256 (019af29f...) matches survey-summary.json.

verdict.reasoning:
I re-checked both files and the auditor's evidence is correct, so I can't refute it. Both C:\Users\<user>\Documents\AlphaRush\runtime\rl\elite-v2\runs\native-final-af081b54e5f54478aa76b24bc02bdbf5\survey-summary.json and C:\Users\<user>\Documents\AlphaRush\runtime\rl\elite-v2\runs\native-final-af081b54e5f54478aa76b24bc02bdbf5\worker-stdout.json are 69455 bytes. Their sha256 hashes start 019af29f2698 and 511d96fd92e3, so they differ. After json.loads the two objects are equal. Both files use CRLF line endings (3514 each) and end with a trailing CRLF.

The bytes first differ at offset 6. survey-summary.json starts with "action_scope" (keys in alphabetical order). worker-stdout.json starts with "schema", "run_id", "policy", "seeds", which is the order the keys were inserted. Ignoring the trailing CRLF, survey-summary.json is exactly json.dumps(obj, sort_keys=True, indent=2) of worker-stdout's content. worker-stdout.json is exactly json.dumps(obj, indent=2) without sorting.

The code explains why. In C:\Users\<user>\Documents\AlphaRush\tools\campaign-survey.py, the worker prints its result with print(json.dumps(value, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)) at line 95, without sort_keys. The supervisor sends that stdout to worker-stdout.json at line 1041. survey-summary.json (SUMMARY, line 82) is written by _write_new_json at lines 97-102, which uses sort_keys=True. So the difference is expected from the code and is not corruption or a mismatch.

supervisor-receipt.json has summary_sha256 = 019af29f26982821..., which matches survey-summary.json, the file the receipt is meant to cover. Nothing in the receipt chain refers to worker-stdout.json's hash. The problem is real but cosmetic, and it does not affect the claimed result.
verdict.corrected_statement: In the final run, worker-stdout.json and survey-summary.json have different bytes (sha256 511d96fd... vs 019af29f...) but are the same size (69455 bytes), have the same CRLF line breaks and parse to identical JSON. The only difference is key order. The worker prints its summary with keys in insertion order (tools/campaign-survey.py line 95, no sort_keys). survey-summary.json is written by _write_new_json with sort_keys=True (lines 97-102). This is how the code is meant to work, not a sign of tampering or a mismatch. The supervisor receipt's summary_sha256 (019af29f...) matches survey-summary.json, the file it is meant to cover. The issue is cosmetic and has no effect on the claimed 120/130 levels or on seed 8101's 26/26.

problems.title: episode_id does not include the seed
problems.evidence: Episode ids such as native-final-...-L01-a0 repeat across the 5 seeds. Pairs of (seed, episode_id) are unique, so the recount is unaffected, but tooling that keys on episode_id alone would merge games from different seeds.

verdict.reasoning:
I streamed the final run's episodes.jsonl read-only and could not refute the claim. It has 1,144 rows: 745 strategy_decision, 267 campaign_attempt, 102 challenge_attempt and 30 star_replay. The 399 rows that carry a game result all have payload.result.episode_id, and result.seed always matches payload.seed. Across those 399 rows there are only 132 distinct episode_ids, and 91 of them appear under two or more seeds. By kind: 62 of 92 campaign_attempt ids, 7 of 13 star_replay ids and 22 of 27 challenge_attempt ids are shared. For example, native-final-af081b54e5f54478aa76b24bc02bdbf5-L01-a0 appears under all five seeds, 8101 to 8105. No id contains a seed number.

The cause is in alpharush_rl/campaign_run.py. Lines 398, 275 and 342 build the ids as f"{ctx.run_id}-L{level:02d}-a{attempt}", "-r{attempt}" and "-m{mode}-a{attempt}". All five seed campaigns share one run_id, so the same level and attempt number gives the same id on every seed.

The auditor is also right that the recount is unaffected. All 399 (seed, episode_id) pairs are distinct, with no duplicates. Counting levels won per seed from campaign_attempt rows gives 8101=26, 8102=25 (missing L22), 8103=22, 8104=25 (missing L22) and 8105=22, for a total of 120. That matches the claim, including seed 8101 winning all 26 levels.

Keying on episode_id alone really would merge games: the 120 winning campaign attempts collapse to 44 distinct ids. However, I found no in-repo consumer that does this. The other occurrences in alpharush_rl, tools and tests either generate ids, put them in the episode trace, or pass them into the policy context. No policy reads context['episode_id']; they seed their random generators from decision_index. The published tools/recording/record_final.py filters by seed before using rows. events.jsonl, survey-summary.json and both receipt files contain no episode_ids. So the defect is real but latent, and it affects only data-hygiene and traceability.
verdict.corrected_statement: Confirmed, minor, with no effect on the claimed result. In the final run native-final-af081b54e5f54478aa76b24bc02bdbf5, alpharush_rl/campaign_run.py builds episode_id as {run_id}-L{level}-a{attempt}, -r{attempt} or -m{mode}-a{attempt}, without the seed, and all five seed campaigns share one run_id. Of the 399 result-bearing rows, there are only 132 distinct episode_ids, and 91 of them are shared by two or more seeds (62 campaign, 7 star-replay, 22 challenge). For example, ...-L01-a0 appears under all of seeds 8101 to 8105. Each row's payload.seed and result.seed agree, and every (seed, episode_id) pair is unique. A recount keyed on (seed, level) reproduces 26/25/22/25/22 = 120 of 130 levels, with seed 8101 at 26/26, so both claims stand. The risk is latent: any tool that keyed on episode_id alone would merge games from different seeds, collapsing the 120 winning attempts to 44 ids. No current in-repo consumer does this; for example, record_final.py filters by seed first.

problems.title: The code's hero rule is looser than the stated project rule (no effect in this run)
problems.evidence: The task says the 7 extra heroes are allowed only after main level 12 is won. campaign.py FREE_HEROES gives them available_level 12, and heroes_available(level) lets level >= 12 through, which matches the game's own gate (#slot.levels >= 12). In the final run none of the 8 main-L12 campaign attempts used an extra hero (all used hero_bolin), so there is no violation. A future plan portfolio could use one on L12 under the code rule.
